cells.tense: You are moving from something felt, and the direction comes with it.
cells.ask: Hand one thing you keep over to someone this week, finished, with no conditions on what they do with it.
cells.core:
When a shared thing is worth passing on, the pull to pass it shows up while you're still in it. You feel a piece of meaning that holds — yours and someone else's — and the next move follows from that, not from a plan. That kind of movement is hard to fake and easy to miss when you're busy.

The part that costs comes after: wanting to check that what you gave landed right, watching how it's used, keeping a hand on it. The connection is real. Holding on is the extra piece, and it's holding on that makes handing something over feel like losing it. Let one carrying be a gift with no receipt.
cells.sheetLine: Direction arrives while you're in it. Trust that part.
cells.verb: merging what's worth carrying toward what's worth joining
cells.place: where a shared meaning is handed down and kept alive

cells.tense: You are trying to lock in a joining that has not fully shown itself yet.
cells.ask: Before the next conversation about it, set down what you want it to become and let it sit unsent for a week.
cells.core:
The future is being written out ahead of the meeting. Before both people know what's actually on the table, the union is assumed and everything gets built around it — plans, shared language, routines, a story of how this will go. Each push looks like commitment, which is why it's hard to catch from inside. It reads as care. It costs the thing care was for.

What's being tended right now is the shape of the joining, arriving before the joining. Ease up and the pull to rush goes with it. What's real here won't need to be forced into place.

cells.tense: You are standing outside something that already happened, still deciding whether to walk in.
cells.ask: Go back to one practice or group you used to belong to, once, even awkwardly, and let no one need to notice.
cells.core:
Something real passed between you and other people, and you've been treating it as a one-off ever since. A genuine meeting and a near one are easy for you to separate, and lately the near ones are the only ones you're letting happen. Nothing is wrong with seeing clearly. It just isn't taking you anywhere.

What's missing is the crossing. You can still read exactly what mattered and what didn't — that part is sharp — but reading it hasn't turned into belonging to anything. Standing back has become its own habit, safer than choosing and safer than being chosen. Seeing things straight is fine. The joining is what stopped.
cells.sheetLine: The meeting already happened. You're the one still outside it.

cells.tense: Something has already carried you toward a shared life, and you keep calling it circumstance.
cells.ask: Name one thing that's yours because of a commitment you made with others, and say so out loud to one person.
cells.core:
A language has formed between you and other people and you didn't sit down to invent it. The way you say things, the bits of history you repeat, the small practices that mean something only to those who were there — all of it is running, and you talk as if it came together on its own.

What's misfiled isn't the fact. Somewhere along the way you did pick this, probably more than once, and the picking has been quietly filed under luck or the mood of the group. Nothing needs renegotiating. The claim just wants to be set down somewhere, so what you carry is also what you stand in.
cells.sheetLine: You built something with people. You've been calling it just how things are.

attempts.check: The claim the record doesn't support is that the person is currently choosing one person or one tradition to belong to — the card is only a transient, so it can be read as a moment they are meeting, not a fact about their ties. A reader could reasonably say they aren't deciding anything right now because nothing has arrived to decide, and the ask is still useful if that's true, since each ask works on what is already in their hands. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that presumes a particular other person or a particular tradition is the subject.
